rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.e1: Attack: in 1858, at the Paris Opera, Paul Morphy played White against the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, who played together. It is White to play on the seventh move.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.e2: To develop a piece is to bring it from its starting square to an active square. Both sides have a pawn in the centre, on e4 and on e5: each controls central squares and opens the way for the pieces. White has developed the bishop and the queen; Black, only the knight on f6.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.e3: Each move is a tempo. Moving the same piece twice or taking it to the edge spends tempi without developing. Whoever falls behind in development gives the other side the chance to attack before they get organised.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.p: White is better developed. Use that advantage now. Find the best move.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.certo: The queen goes to b3 and attacks the pawn on b7 and the pawn on f7 at the same time, and the bishop on c4 also attacks f7. It is a double attack.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.revela: The best move was the queen to b3: she attacks the pawn on b7 and the pawn on f7 at the same time, and the bishop on c4 also attacks f7.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.err.c4f7: The bishop captures the pawn on f7 with check.
With this move Black has a resource: the king recaptures the bishop, and White is left with a pawn for a piece.
Back to the position: look for a move that attacks two targets at the same time without giving up a piece.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.fora: That move does not use the advantage right now. Developing one more piece, for example, is natural, but it gives Black time to get organised. Look for a move that attacks two targets at the same time.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.volta: Try again: look for the double attack.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l0: Black must defend both pawns with a single move.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l1: The black queen goes to e7 and defends the pawn on f7. The pawn on b7 is left undefended, and the black queen leaves home without developing another piece.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l2: The knight goes to c3 and develops one more piece. Capturing the pawn on b7 with the queen also won, but Morphy preferred to gain one more tempo.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l3: The c7 pawn advances one square and opens the seventh rank, and the queen on e7 now defends the pawn on b7.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l4: The bishop goes to g5, develops and pins the knight on f6 to the queen on e7.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex1.l5: White has four pieces in play; Black has two, and the black king is still in the centre. Morphy gave mate on the 17th move.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.e1: Defence: now in a Caro-Kann game played on Lichess. White has not castled yet, and the bishop on b5 has no defender.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.e2: In positions like this, developing and castling are good plans, but the opponent's concrete threat comes first.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.p: Several moves work here. Find a move that does not lose material.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.certo: With that move, the black queen on a5 wins no material. Castling, for example, takes the king off the a5 diagonal.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.revela: A good move was castling: the king leaves the a5 diagonal, and the black queen cannot win the bishop with check.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.h2h3: The h2 pawn advances: it is a rook-pawn move, which develops no piece, and the bishop on b5 still has no defender.
With this move Black has a resource: the queen goes to a5, gives check and attacks the bishop on b5 at the same time, and the bishop falls.
Back to the position: before choosing the move, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.a2a3: The a2 pawn advances: it is a rook-pawn move, which develops no piece, and the bishop on b5 still has no defender.
With this move Black has a resource: the queen goes to a5, gives check and attacks the bishop on b5 at the same time, and the bishop falls.
Back to the position: before choosing the move, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.c1f4: The bishop goes to f4 and develops, but the bishop on b5 still has no defender against a check.
With this move Black has a resource: the queen goes to a5, gives check and attacks the bishop on b5 at the same time, and the bishop falls.
Back to the position: before choosing the move, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.c1e3: The bishop goes to e3 and develops, but the bishop on b5 still has no defender against a check.
With this move Black has a resource: the queen goes to a5, gives check and attacks the bishop on b5 at the same time, and the bishop falls.
Back to the position: before choosing the move, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.c1g5: The bishop goes to g5 and develops, but the bishop on b5 still has no defender against a check.
With this move Black has a resource: the queen goes to a5, gives check and attacks the bishop on b5 at the same time, and the bishop falls.
Back to the position: before choosing the move, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.err.f3e5: The knight goes to e5 and attacks the knight on c6 again, but it is the second time it moves.
With this move Black has a resource: the knight on c6 captures on e5, and the bishop on d7 now attacks the bishop on b5. White loses a piece.
Back to the position: the bishop on b5 has no defender. Before choosing the move, check which black pieces can attack it.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.fora: That move leaves material behind. Before choosing, see what the black queen attacks from a5.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.volta: Try again: look at Black's threat first.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.l1: With castling, the king leaves the a5 diagonal and is safe. If the black queen goes to a5, the bishop on b5 has time to retreat.
rot.openingPrinciples.ideia.ex2.l2: In the game, White advanced the h2 pawn and lost the bishop to the queen check on a5. The principle applies after checking the threat.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.londres.1: Attack: now with Black, in a London System game between titled players. The white queen has already moved several times and has just captured the pawn on a7.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.londres.2: The bishop goes to c5, develops and attacks the queen. She has no square: the black pieces and the king cover every exit.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.londres.3: Trapped, the white queen gives herself up: she captures the bishop, and this is the defence that loses least.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.londres.4: The rook recaptures on c5. Black wins the queen for a bishop: the queen that came out early and moved many times was hunted down.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.caroKann.1: Attack: Black again, in a Caro-Kann game played on Lichess. The white knight moved again and went to the edge, on h4, with no defender.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.caroKann.2: The queen goes to b4, gives check and attacks the knight on h4 along the fourth rank. It is a double attack.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.caroKann.3: The c2 pawn advances, blocks and attacks the queen, but it does not defend the knight.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.caroKann.4: The queen captures the knight on h4, and Black wins a piece. The time spent putting the knight on the edge cost dearly.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.1: Defence: now with Black, in the Two Knights Defence. The white pawn has just captured on d5, the knight on c6 is attacked, and Black is a pawn down.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.2: The knight goes to a5, escapes and attacks the bishop on c4. The knight moves for the second time and goes to the edge, against the principle.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.3: The bishop goes to b5 and saves itself with check. The check forces Black's reply: a move with check or with an attack, played first, gains a tempo.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.4: The c7 pawn advances, blocks and attacks the bishop again.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.5: The d5 pawn captures the pawn on c6.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.6: The b7 pawn recaptures on c6 and attacks the bishop for the third time.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.7: The bishop retreats to e2. White has spent many moves with the bishop and the knight on g5, and Black develops with tempo.
rot.openingPrinciples.demos.excecao.8: Back to the position: here the knight moved twice and went to the edge, and this is the main line. In this position, the move that attacks the bishop does not lose time.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.ataque.enu: Now with White, in a game played on Lichess. Black is two pawns up, but the black queen came out early to h4, and the other black pieces are still at home. Play as White and find the best move.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.ataque.fim: The bishop developed and attacked the queen, who came out early and has no safe square. Here, the move that develops with an attack wins the queen that came out early.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.ataque.err: The pawn recaptures on e4, but the black queen captures on e4 with check, and Black remains two pawns up. Look for a move that develops while attacking the queen.
The knight develops and attacks the pawn on e4, but the black queen stays active on h4, and Black remains two pawns up. Look for a move that develops while attacking the queen.
The pawn attacks the queen, but she retreats, and the pawn move develops no piece. Look for a move that attacks the queen and develops a piece at the same time.
The bishop develops, but on f4 it does not attack the queen, and she stays active on h4. Look for another square for the bishop.
That move does not attack the black queen, and she stays active on h4. Black remains two pawns up. Look for a move that develops while attacking the queen.
That move does not attack the black queen, and she stays active on h4. Black remains two pawns up. Look for a move that develops while attacking the queen.
That move does not attack the black queen, and she stays active on h4. Black remains two pawns up. Look for a move that develops while attacking the queen.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.valeAqui.e: Now with White, in the Stafford Defence. The bishop on c5 and the knight on f6 aim at f2 and e4. Is it worth developing the bishop on c1 now? Play as White and find the best move.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.valeAqui.f: The bishop on f1 developed, defended your kingside and prepared castling. White keeps the advantage.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.valeAqui.e: The bishop develops, but Black exchanges it for the bishop on c5, and White's advantage shrinks. Look for the move that develops a piece and protects the kingside.
The knight develops, but the knight on f6 jumps to g4 and attacks f2 together with the bishop on c5. Before developing, take care of f2.
The bishop develops, but the knight on f6 captures the pawn on e4 and attacks your bishop and f2 at the same time. Check the threat before developing.
Now with White, in a Caro-Kann game. Your bishop on a6 is far from home, and the pawn on b5 takes away one of its escape squares. Play as White and find the best move.
You did not lose the bishop. The rook-pawn advance, which looks natural, let the black queen give check and attack the bishop at the same time.
The knight develops, but the black queen gives check on a5 and attacks your bishop on a6 at the same time. Take care of the bishop before the check.
The knight develops, but the black queen gives check on a5 and attacks your bishop on a6 at the same time. Take care of the bishop before the check.
The rook pawn attacks the pawn on b5, but the black queen gives check and attacks your bishop at the same time. Take care of the bishop before the check.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.damaCedo.e: Now with Black, in a London System game. The pawn on f3 attacks your knight on e4. Play as Black and find the best move.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.damaCedo.f: The knight got out of the attack, and you lost no material. The queen check looked strong, but a pawn drove her away, and the knight was lost.
rot.openingPrinciples.pratica.damaCedo.e: The knight on d7 captures on e5, but the pawn recaptures, and your knight on e4 is still attacked by the pawn on f3. Get the knight on e4 out of the attack first.
The pawn advances and attacks the bishop on d3, but the f3 pawn captures your knight on e4. Get the knight out of the attack first.
The bishop develops, but the f3 pawn captures your knight on e4. Get the knight out of the attack first.
The queen comes out early and gives check, but a pawn attacks her, and your knight on e4 is still attacked: you lose a piece. Get the knight out of the attack first.
